name: sfst
desc: Toolbox for morphological analysers and other FST-based tools
why: A toolbox for finite-state transducers that build morphological analysers, a door into how computers parse words in language.

brief.what_it_is: SFST is a C++ toolbox for building morphological analysers and other tools based on finite state transducers. According to its homepage it has four parts: a compiler that turns transducer programs into minimised transducers, interactive and batch-mode analysis programs, tools for comparing and printing transducers, and an efficient C++ transducer library. The homepage does not say explicitly what goes in and what comes out, but the compiler takes transducer source programs and the analysis tools run transducers over input text. The executables in the brew metadata (fst-compiler, fst-mor, fst-infl2, fst-generate and others) fit that description, but I did not verify them against any documentation.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it as a way to implement morphological analysers and other FST-based tools. The author says it is easy for people who already know grep, sed, or Perl to pick up.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage gives only a high-level picture: transducer programs are compiled into minimised transducers, which are then run by analysis programs or the C++ library. It does not explain the transducer programming language or the analysis pipeline in detail. The README and manual were not reachable from the homepage text, so those details are missing.
brief.install_notes: The homepage offers source code downloads, with the latest listed as version 1.4.7g. Community packaging is linked: a Debian package by Francis Tyers and a Homebrew formula for Macs contributed by Nathan Glenn. No build steps, dependencies, or first-run instructions appear on the homepage. The brew formula is the route the catalogue is using here.
brief.standout: It is a long-lived, GPL-licensed FST toolkit that the homepage presents as a base for other projects. The page lists HFST, which was built on top of SFST, OpenFST, and foma, and AFST, which is based on SFST. It also points to real morphologies built with it, including SMOR (German), LatMor (Latin), EMOR (English), TRMOR (Turkish), mlmorph (Malayalam), and yakutmorph (Yakut).
brief.status: Unknown in terms of dates. The homepage lists version 1.4.7g as the newest download, described as 'only minor changes', with earlier entries going back to 1.2. No release dates or commit information appear on the page, and I did not check a repository. The changelog-style list and the contributed packages suggest it has been maintained for years, but I cannot confirm recent activity from what I read.
brief.caveats: The homepage is thin: it has no install commands, no usage examples, and no README content. Commands, dependencies, and platform support could not be checked from it. The author's contact address is given as a placeholder that must be edited by hand to avoid spam harvesting. Weighted transducer support is described as 'basic functionality only'. The brew executables list was supplied by the catalogue metadata and was not confirmed on the page.
quotes: SFST is a toolbox for the implementation of morphological analysers and other tools which are based on finite state transducer technology.
easy to learn for users who are familiar with grep, sed, or Perl.
freely available under the GNU Public License
fetch_log: https://www.cis.uni-muenchen.de/~schmid/tools/SFST/ - fetched OK; returned the homepage text (not a GitHub README). The page links to the manual, the FSMNLP 2005 paper, and downloads, but the fetched text did not include their URLs, so I did not follow them.
